title: attention-kernel-optimization-profiling-flashattention-paged-fused-notes-2026-03-17
content:
Summary:

Notes from profiling runs focused on attention kernel performance across three optimization strategies: FlashAttention (FA), paged attention (PA), and fused attention ops (FO). Goal was to identify dominant bottlenecks at inference time for medium-to-long sequences (512-2048) on A100 and H100 variants, and produce concrete recommendations for runtime kernel selection and fallback policies.

Environment:
- HW: NVIDIA A100 40GB (SXM), H100 80GB (SXM) for a subset of runs.
- SW: PyTorch 2.2 + custom CUDA kernels, cuBLAS/cuDNN versions consistent with driver 535.x, libcudnn 9.x.
- Runtime: Redwood serving runtime commit @ feature/attention-op-optim (PR 678). Test harness based on synthetic and real prompt distributions.
- Tools: Nsight Systems (nsys), Nsight Compute (ncu), PyTorch profiler (CUDA mode), CUPTI counters, nvprof (legacy for quick sanity checks), custom micro-bench timers (cudaEvent timings).

Workloads and models:
- Decoder-only transformer, medium (1.2B) and large-ish (13B) variants; layer config representative of customer workloads.
- Sequence lengths tested: 512, 1024, 1536, 2048. Batch sizes: 1, 4, 8 (with padding where needed).
- Common patterns: many short requests (seq <=512) and occasional long-context requests (>=1024) - important for cache/paging behavior.

Profiling methodology:
1) Microbench kernels in isolation (single-layer attention forward) to measure pure kernel latency and memory traffic.
2) End-to-end generation loop (full model) to capture KV cache behavior and host-device memcopies.
3) Tracing under load to observe scheduler interactions (kernel launch overhead, queue depth, concurrency with other streams).
4) Compare FA, PA, and FO variants with identical inputs and same CUDA launch config where applicable.
5) Capture hardware counters: achieved occupancy, SM utilization, DRAM throughput, L2 hit rate, warp efficiency, and instruction mix.

Key observations:
- FlashAttention (FA):
  - Pros: consistently lowest single-kernel latency for short-to-medium sequences on H100 due to optimized memory layout and fused softmax. High arithmetic intensity reduces DRAM pressure.
  - Cons: For very long sequences (>=1536), FA's working set can exceed shared memory / register tiling assumptions leading to higher L2 traffic and occasional kernel reconfiguration with worse occupancy. Also sensitive to batch size and padding; if sequence lengths vary a lot, performance regresses.

- Paged Attention (PA):
  - Pros: Good for long contexts because it explicitly pages KV cache tiles and avoids holding full KV in shared memory. Lower peak memory consumption and more predictable DRAM patterns. Latency scales more gracefully with sequence length.
  - Cons: Higher kernel launch overhead (more smaller kernels), increased host-device synchronization in our current implementation, and suboptimal utilization for short sequences. Paging introduces additional memcpy patterns that show up in traces.

- Fused Ops (FO):
  - Pros: Combines multiple operator stages (query matmul, attention score, softmax, value matmul) into fewer kernels - reduces kernel launch overhead and intermediate memory writes. For batch sizes >=4 FO yields strong end-to-end throughput improvements.
  - Cons: Implementation complexity: edge cases (masked attention, rotary embeddings, past key/value concat) required additional code paths that occasionally force de-optimization. FO performance depends heavily on register pressure and can drop on architectures with different register file sizes.

Bottleneck breakdowns (representative run: 13B, seq=1536, batch=1 on A100):
- FA: kernel compute dominated (~70% of attention wall time), but L2 bandwidth climbs near device peak in peaks. Softmax/final reductions are compute heavy but fused; KV staging costs small.
- PA: DRAM bandwidth and memcpy overhead ~45% of attention time; kernel compute ~35%; kernel launch overhead ~15% (many small kernels).
- FO: kernel launch overhead lower (~5%), compute ~60%, register spilling to local memory caused by high register pressure accounted for a noticeable perf drop in particular layers (~10%).

Surprising finds / regression sources:
- Host-device memcpy interleaving: Our current KV cache implementation triggers synchronous page writes for PA in the critical path for some request sizes. Switching to async copies with CUDA streams reduced observed tail latency by ~18% in PA runs.
- Kernel launch latency: For PA, many small kernels (tile ops) exacerbate CPU-side scheduling; switching to batched launches and using persistent kernel patterns lowered overhead.
- Mixed-arch tuning: FA kernels tuned for H100 show regressions on A100 due to different optimal tile sizes. Need per-arch kernel selection at runtime.
- Softmax numerical path: FA fused softmax uses an alternative numerics path for stability; in some prompt patterns outputs differed slightly (in the 1e-6 range) - acceptable for inference but flagged in regression tests.

Quantitative summary (single inference median latencies, normalized):
- Short seq (512), batch=1: FA best (1.0x baseline), FO ~1.05x, PA ~1.3x.
- Medium seq (1024), batch=1: FA ~1.0x, FO ~1.08x, PA ~1.18x.
- Long seq (1536), batch=1: PA ~1.0x, FA ~1.08x (with occasional spikes), FO ~1.12x.
- Very long seq (2048), batch=1: PA ~1.0x, FA ~1.2x, FO ~1.15x.
- Batch=4 throughput: FO leads for medium seq (up to 8-12% better throughput than FA), since kernel fusion reduces overhead; PA improves marginally with batching but not enough to beat fused kernels.

Recommendations for runtime policy:
1) Kernel selection policy by request profile (sequence length + batch size):
   - If seq <= 1024 and batch <= 1: prefer FlashAttention on H100/A100 (where available).
   - If seq between 1024-1536: prefer FA for H100, PA for A100 unless batchable (batch>=4) then FO is attractive.
   - If seq >=1536: prefer Paged Attention for predictable latency, unless model footprint is small and FA tuned for the architecture.
2) Use architecture-aware kernel registry: at startup detect GPU generation and choose tuned kernels (tile sizes, block dims).
3) Implement async KV page IO for PA to avoid syncs on critical paths.
4) Provide a hybrid fallback: try FA first, monitor latency and L2 usage; if we hit defined thresholds (L2 BW > 85% or tail latency > x ms), fallback to PA for that session.
5) Expose a per-model config for fused ops toggle with safety checks to disable for models using uncommon ops (rotary+mask combos) where FO de-optimizes.

Next experiments / TODOs:
- Run extended stability suite with real customer prompts to surface rare numerical deltas between FA and PA/FO.
- Implement persistent kernel variant for PA to amortize launch overhead and re-profile.
- Expand profiling to multi-tenant scenarios to measure interference (L2/DMA contention).
- Automate kernel selection tuning: run microbench on first warmup and cache preferred kernel per instance.

Appendix (quick run checklist):
- Reproduce cmd (microbench): python tools/attention_microbench.py --model 13B --seq 1536 --batch 1 --kernel flashattention --device a100
- Trace command (nsys): nsys profile --output=trace.nsys --trace=cuda,osrt python serving/runtime_benchmark.py --workload long_context
- Nsight compute example: ncu --target-processes all --set full --metrics achieved_occupancy,sm__throughput_avg,dram__throughput ./bin/attention_kernel_test

Notes to reviewers:
- I left raw trace artifacts under GCS: gs://redwood-profiling/2026-03-17/ (index in Confluence page).
- See PR 678 for current PA async-copy changes; still WIP and needs unit tests around masked attention.

End of note.
